content: The study involved several datasets focusing on cervical cancer screening and diagnosis among women living with HIV (WLHIV) and HIV-negative women. Below is a detailed breakdown of the findings and methodologies: 1. Study Populations and Screening Methods: Smita Joshi conducted a cohort study involving 1,154 women, all HIV-positive, screened using cytology, HPV testing, visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA), and colposcopy. Of these, 135 underwent confirmation biopsies. Thida Chanyachukul analyzed data from 191 women in Thailand screened with cytology, of whom 92 were HIV-positive. No confirmation biopsies were performed. Simon Manga utilized routine clinical care data from Cameroon (2012–2019), where 68,232 women were screened using VIA, and 698 underwent confirmation biopsies. Among these, 8,539 were HIV-positive. Across all datasets, there were 12,527 HIV-positive participants and 49,365 HIV-negative participants. 2. Data Harmonization and Analysis: The datasets were reviewed individually and harmonized by mapping variables to a master list provided by the World Health Organization (WHO). Discrepancies were resolved with investigators before combining the datasets. A one-stage individual patient data meta-analysis (IPD-MA) was conducted using random intercept models to account for study heterogeneity. Generalized linear mixed models were applied to analyze cervical screening test responses, with diagnostics and goodness-of-fit assessed through statistical tools. 3. Key Findings: Among WLHIV aged 15–19, 20–24, 25–29, and 30–34, the probabilities of a confirmed diagnosis of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia grade 2 or 3 (CIN2/3) were 6%, 32%, 42%, and 50%, respectively. Subgroup analysis focused on cases with histopathological confirmation. Predicted probabilities of histopathological diagnoses were stratified by age and HIV status. Only 6% of women had their screening test results confirmed by histopathology from biopsies. 4. Screening Test Results: Among WLHIV, the availability of histopathological diagnoses varied by screening method: Cytology: 1,978 tests with histopathology available. HPV testing: 1,916 tests with histopathology available. VIA: 1,514 tests with histopathology available. A total of 5,408 screening tests among WLHIV had histopathological confirmation. 5. Challenges and Limitations: Discordant test results were highlighted, emphasizing the need for improved diagnostic accuracy. The study noted that only a small proportion of women had histopathological confirmation, which may limit the generalizability of findings. 6. Survey on Acceptability and Preferences: A global online survey was conducted to assess the acceptability and preferences for cervical cancer screening and treatment among women, including WLHIV. The survey received 561 responses from 68 countries, with the majority of participants being well-educated. However, there was a potential selection bias due to the online nature of the survey. Key findings included: 51% of women in the general population had undergone at least one screening test, compared to 75% of WLHIV who had received multiple tests. Many women expressed discomfort with the use of a speculum during screening and preferred less invasive methods. There was a strong preference for immediate treatment following a diagnosis of cervical intraepithelial lesions, with 82% of the general population and 75% of WLHIV favoring this approach. 7. Barriers to Screening and Follow-Up: WLHIV reported more challenges in attending screening programs compared to the general population (42% vs. 17%). Common barriers included work-related issues, fear of pain, and a perception of low risk for cervical cancer. Despite these challenges, many women emphasized the importance of their health and expressed a willingness to return for follow-up care. 8. Recommendations and Conclusions: The study highlighted the need for accessible, less invasive screening methods and better counseling services to address patient concerns. It emphasized the importance of immediate treatment following diagnosis and the need for tailored interventions to improve screening attendance among WLHIV. This comprehensive analysis provides valuable insights into the challenges and preferences surrounding cervical cancer screening and treatment, particularly among WLHIV, and offers actionable recommendations to improve care delivery.
